source_text: τοῦ μονογενοῦς θεότητος· καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν τοιούτων δείκνυται κρίσεως, αὐτὸ τῇ φύσει ἁγιότης καὶ ἀγαθότης καὶ δύναμις ὑπάρχον, ἅτε ἓν ὂν ἐκ τοῦ ἑνός. ἐπεὶ πρὸς τὴν ἐκείνων ἐρισχελίαν οὔτε ὁ ἀγαθώτατος καὶ ἵλεως τὴν φύσιν υἱὸς ἔτι ἀγαθὸς ἔσται· ἐπειδὴ μὴ συνηνωμένον ἔχει τὸ «εἷς θεός». οὔτε μὴν ὁ φιλανθρωπότατος καὶ ὅλος ἵλεως πατὴρ καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ἕξουσιν ἐπίσημα τὰ μνημονευθέντα ὀνόματα τῆς θεότητος· ἀλλὰ καὶ δι' αὐτῶν ὑποβιβασθήσονται οἷον, ὡς ἔθος λαλεῖν αἱρετικοῖς, εἰς τοὺς ὁμωνύμους ἡμᾶς. ἵλαθι δέ, ἁγία τριάς. –ἀλλ' ὁ υἱός, φησίν, συναπογεννηθεὶς ἔμφυτον ἔχει τὴν ἀγαθότητα, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ὅσα ὁ πατήρ. –ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα συνεκπορευθὲν κατὰ φύσιν ἐστὶν ἀγαθόν, καὶ ὅσα ὁ θεὸς πατήρ. 3.30 εἰ μὲν οὖν περὶ τῶν τυχόντων ἢ βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων ἦν αὐτοῖς ἡ διάλεξις, καλῶς ἂν αὐτοῖς ἐσθότε χρεία ἐγίνετο συμπλάσσειν μύθους τινάς, καὶ Ἀριστοτελικῇ δῆθεν δεινότητι καὶ τῇ ἐν λόγοις τέχνῃ, ὡς Εὐνόμιος, περιστρέφειν τὸ πρᾶγμα καὶ συσκιάζειν τὴν ἀλήθειαν· 3.31 νῦν δὲ διδάσκει Παῦλος· «ἐὰν μὴ πιστεύσητε, οὐδ' οὐ μὴ συνῆτε,» καί· «ἡ σοφία τῶν ἀνθρώπων μωρία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ.» καὶ οὐ χρὴ τὰ περὶ τοῦ ἐνδόξου πνεύματος λόγια τὰ μείζονα λογισμῶν ἀνθρωπίνων κατασοφίζεσθαι. οὐ γὰρ βλάπτει ψόγος τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, οὐδὲ περαιτέρω τῆς ἀκοῆς προέρχονται οἱ ὀνειδισμοὶ καὶ τὰ σκώμματα τῶν αἱρετικῶν, οἷς ἐπῆλθε τὸ φαύλως φρονεῖν· ἀλλ' οἱ χρώμενοι τοιούτοις ἀπέραντα πονήσουσιν καὶ πράξουσιν παραπλήσιά πως τοῖς ἐπιχειροῦσιν ἀποσκώπτειν εἰς τοῦτο τὸ φῶς, τὸ ἐκ τοῦ ἀπροσίτου φωτὸς τὴν ἴσχυν ἔχον, καὶ μιαίνειν τοῖς λόγοις αὐτό. 3.32 πιστεύειν δὲ δεῖ τὴν ἐκ τῶν ἁγίων διδασκαλίαν τῆς παρ' ἀνθρώπων πλείονα δύνασθαι τὴν δόξαν ἐμποιεῖν. ἡμῖν τοίνυν ἁρμόζει ἐκείνοις ἐπιμέμφεσθαι τοῦ μὴ δι' ὑπερβολὴν εὐνοίας τῆς περὶ τὴν οἰκείαν αἵρεσιν καθέλκειν τό γε ἐπ' αὐτοῖς τὸ θεῖον εἰς τὰ τῶν κτισμάτων ἀποτελέσματα ταῖς σοφιστείαις, καὶ διὰ τούτων τίκτειν ἀπωλείας ἔρωτα τοῖς ἁπλουστέροις καὶ ἀπειροτέροις, καὶ προάγειν εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν ἁμαρτημάτων μειζόνων. 4.ν Περὶ τῶν λεγόντων αἱρετικῶν· πνεῦμα ὁ θεός· καὶ πῶς τοῦ πνεύματος πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμά ἐστιν; καὶ πάλιν· οἱ ἄγγελοι οὖν, φασίν, οὐκ εἰσὶν ἀπὸ θεοῦ καὶ ἅγιοι καὶ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ; 4.1 Ἀλλ' ἀποπεμπόμενοι μὲν τὰ ἁπλᾶ καὶ εὐθέα καὶ τέλεια καὶ ἀνεπιστημοσύνης ἀναπιμπλῶντες τῶν ἱερῶν λόγων τὴν προαίρεσιν, καθ' ἣν ἐθέλει ὁ θεὸς πατὴρ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ συντάττεσθαι αὐτῷ, ὡς τὸν μονογενῆ λόγον, καὶ τὸ ἐξῃρημένον αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς κτίσεως καὶ ὑπερέχον ἀσφαλίζεται, διὸ καὶ τρισαγιολογεῖται, φασίν· πῶς τοῦ πνεύματος πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμά ἐστιν; 4.2 ὅτι δὲ τοῦτο γέγραπται, δέδεικται· τὸ δὲ πῶς, νοῦ καὶ λόγου τοῦ καθ' ἡμᾶς, ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἀγγέλων γνώσεως ἐπέκεινα τυγχάνει. ὡς γὰρ πατρὸς ὑπάρχοντος αὐτοῦ, ἐγεννήθη ἐξ αὐτοῦ ὁ θεὸς λόγος· οὕτως ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ ἐξεφάνη τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα· δείκνυταί τε ἐν τούτῳ μάλιστα τὸ ἀκατάληπτον αὐτοῦ, ἐν τῷ τὸ φαινόμενον καὶ ὂν τῇ κτίσει ἀδύνατον εἶναι παρ' αὐτῷ δυνατόν. ἐπεὶ τίς ἡ διαφορὰ τῆς ἀναιτίου καὶ ζωοποιοῦ φύσεως καὶ τῆς δημιουργηθείσης καὶ ζωοποιουμένης; οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖ δὲ τὸ 49 πνεῦμα μὴ εἶναι ὁμοούσιον καὶ ἰσότιμον ἐκείνου, ἐξ οὗ ἐστιν. διόπερ ἐστὶν καὶ ἅγιον φυσικῶς. 4.3 οἱ οὖν ἄγγελοι, φησίν, οὐκ εἰσὶν ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἅγιοι καὶ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ; ἐκεῖνοί εἰσιν ἀπὸ θεοῦ, καθ' ὃ προστάξει αὐτοῦ γεγόνασιν, ὡς πάντα· ἅγιοι δὲ μετὰ τὸ ἁγιασθῆναι, ὡς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· πνεύματα δέ, καθὸ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀσώματοι· 4.4 οὐ κληθέντες πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ ἐκπορευόμενα παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἢ θεῖα ἢ πνεύματα ἀληθείας ἢ πνεύματα ἁγιοσύνης· ἀλλ' ἄγγελοι λειτουργοὶ καὶ σώματα οὐράνια διὰ τὸ ἀπείρως ἀπέχειν καὶ ὑφιζάνειν τοῦ ἀκτίστου πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ, κατὰ τὸν γράφοντα ἔμπειρον ἀπόστολον· «σώματα ἐπίγεια καὶ σώματα ἐπουράνια». 4.5 ὡς γὰρ οὐ κατ' αὐτοὺς τὰ πνεύματα τῶν ἀνέμων, οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ κατὰ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ. αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἐκτίσθησαν, οὐ μέντοι ἐξεπορεύθησαν ἐκ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρός· οὐκ ἀναγεννῶσιν ἡμᾶς, οὐ θεοποιοῦσιν, ἁμαρτίας οὐ συγχωροῦσιν, οὐ ζωοποιοῦσιν, οὐ δημιουργοῦσιν, οὐχ ἁγιάζουσιν, οὐ κρίνουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ κρίνονται. «ὑμεῖς» γάρ, φησίν, «καὶ ἀγγέλους κρινεῖτε». 4.6 οὐδ' ἐν αὐτοῖς εἰσιν τῶν οὐρανῶν αἱ δυνάμεις. οὐ τόποις εἰσὶν ἀπερίγραφοι καὶ διαστήμασιν ἀμέτρητοι. ὁ γὰρ Γαβριὴλ λαλῶν τῷ ∆ανιήλ, ἢ εὐαγγελιζόμενος τὴν θεοτόκον
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing: the Holy Spirit is like and equal to the Godhead of the Father and] of the only-begotten; and from the judging of such things it is shown that he himself is by nature holiness and goodness and power, inasmuch as he is one from the one. Since, by their quarrelsome argument, not even the most good and by nature merciful Son will any longer be good, since he does not have 'one God' united with it. Nor indeed will the most loving toward mankind and wholly merciful Father and the Son have the names of the Godhead that were mentioned as distinctive marks; but through them too they will be brought down, as it were, as it is the custom of heretics to talk, to us who bear the same names. Be gracious, Holy Trinity. But the Son, he says, having been begotten together, has goodness inborn, and the other things, as many as the Father has. But the Holy Spirit too, having proceeded together, is by nature good, and as many things as God the Father has. 3.30 If, then, their debate were about chance or everyday matters, it would well have come about as a need for them at times to fashion some fables, and with a cleverness Aristotelian, of course, and the skill in arguments, like Eunomius, to turn the matter about and overshadow the truth; 3.31 but as it is, Paul teaches: 'if you do not believe, neither will you understand', and: 'the wisdom of men is foolishness with God'. And one must not use sophistry on the sayings about the glorious Spirit, which are greater than human reasonings. For blame does not harm the Holy Spirit, nor do the reproaches and gibes of the heretics, on whom thinking badly has come, go forward further than the hearing; but those who use such things will labour without end and will do things somewhat like those who attempt to jeer at this light, which has its strength from the unapproachable light, and to defile it with their words. 3.32 And one must believe that the teaching from the saints is able to instil conviction more than that from men. It befits us therefore to rebuke them, so that they do not, through excess of goodwill toward their own heresy, drag down, as far as lies with them, the divine into the finished works of creatures by their sophistries, and through these beget a love of destruction in the simpler and more inexperienced, and lead them forward into a desire for greater sins. 4.ν [Chapter title:] About the heretics who say: God is spirit; and how is the Holy Spirit spirit of the Spirit? And again: the angels then, they say, are they not from God and holy and spirits of God? 4.1 But sending away the simple and straight and complete things, and filling with lack of knowledge the purpose of the sacred words, according to which God the Father wills his Spirit to be ranked together with him, like the only-begotten Word, and secures his being set apart from creation and surpassing it, for which reason he is also proclaimed thrice holy, they say: how is the Holy Spirit spirit of the Spirit? 4.2 That this has been written has been shown; but the how lies beyond our mind and reason, and further beyond the knowledge of angels too. For as, he being Father, God the Word was begotten from him, so from him and with him the Holy Spirit was made to shine forth; and in this especially is shown his incomprehensibility, in that what appears to be and is impossible for creation is possible with him. Since what is the difference between the uncaused and life-making nature and the one that was crafted and is being made alive? And it is not admissible for the Spirit not to be of the same substance and of equal honour with that one from whom he is. For this reason he is also holy by nature. 4.3 The angels then, he says, are they not from God and holy and spirits of God? Those are from God, in that they came to be by his command, as all things; and holy after being made holy, as men are; and spirits, in that relative to us they are bodiless; 4.4 not having been called spirits of God or out of God or proceeding from the Father or divine or spirits of truth or spirits of holiness; but serving angels and heavenly bodies, because of standing infinitely apart from and sitting below the uncreated Spirit of God, according to the experienced apostle who writes: 'earthly bodies and heavenly bodies'. 4.5 For as the spirits of the winds are not on their level, neither are they on the level of the Holy Spirit of God. For they were created, but did not proceed out of the hypostasis of God and Father; they do not beget us again, do not make us divine, do not forgive sins, do not make alive, do not craft, do not make holy, do not judge, but are even judged. 'For you', he says, 'will judge even angels'. 4.6 Nor in themselves are the powers of the heavens. They are not uncircumscribed by places and unmeasured in extents. For Gabriel, speaking to Daniel, or announcing good news to the God-bearing [virgin, the sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … the Only-begotten’s Godhead. And from a judgment of these things it is shown that he is by nature holiness and goodness and power, since he is one from the one. For by their wrangling, not even the Son, who is most good and merciful by nature, will be good any longer, since he does not have “one God” joined to his name. Nor indeed will the Father, who loves mankind above all and is wholly merciful, and the Son keep the names of the Godhead just mentioned as their own marks; but by these very names they will be brought down, so to speak, as heretics are in the habit of saying, to us who share the names. Be gracious, Holy Trinity!

“But the Son,” they say, “was begotten together with his goodness and has it inborn, and all else that the Father has.” But the Holy Spirit too proceeded together with it and is good by nature, and has all that God the Father has.

If, then, their dispute were about ordinary matters or the affairs of daily life, it might well have been needful for them at times to make up some tales, and, with a cleverness that is Aristotelian, of course, and with skill in arguments, like Eunomius, to twist the matter round and cast a shadow over the truth. But as it is, Paul teaches: “If you do not believe, neither will you understand” (Isaiah 7:9 LXX), and, “The wisdom of men is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). We must not play the sophist with the sayings about the glorious Spirit, which are greater than human reasonings.

For blame does not harm the Holy Spirit, and the reproaches and gibes of the heretics, on whom wrong thinking has come, go no further than the ear. Rather, those who use such words will labour without end, and will do something like those who try to jeer at this light, which has its strength from the inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16), and to defile it with their words.

We must believe that the teaching that comes from the saints has more power to instil conviction than teaching from men. So it befits us to rebuke them, so that they may not, out of excessive goodwill toward their own heresy, drag the divine down, as far as lies with them, among the finished works of creation by their sophistries; nor through these beget a love of perdition in the simpler and less experienced, and lead them on to the desire of greater sins.
Against the heretics who say, “God is spirit” (John 4:24), “and how is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of a spirit?” and again, “Are not the angels, then, from God, and holy, and spirits of God?”

But they set aside what is simple and straightforward and complete, and they fill with ignorance the intent of the sacred words, by which God the Father wills that his Spirit be ranked with him, as the only-begotten Word is, and by which he makes sure that the Spirit is set apart from creation and stands above it; for this reason too he is hailed as thrice holy. And then they say, “How is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of a spirit?”

That this is written has been shown. But the how lies beyond our mind and reason, and even beyond the knowledge of the angels. For as God the Word was begotten from him, since he is Father, so from him and with him the Holy Spirit came forth into light. And in this above all his incomprehensibility is shown: that what appears, and is, impossible for creation is possible with him. Otherwise, what difference would there be between the nature that is uncaused and gives life and the nature that was fashioned and is given life? It is not possible that the Spirit should not be consubstantial and equal in honour with him from whom he is. That is why he is also holy by nature.

“Are not the angels, then,” they say, “from God, and holy, and spirits of God?” They are from God in that they came into being at his command, as all things did; holy once they have been sanctified, as men are; and spirits in that, compared with us, they are bodiless. They have not been called spirits of God, or from God, or proceeding from the Father, or divine, or spirits of truth, or spirits of holiness, but ministering angels and heavenly bodies, because they stand infinitely far from the uncreated Spirit of God and far beneath him. So the experienced apostle writes: “earthly bodies and heavenly bodies” (1 Corinthians 15:40).

For as the spirits of the winds are not on their level, so neither are they on the level of the Holy Spirit of God. For they were created; they did not proceed from the hypostasis of God and Father. They do not regenerate us, they do not make us divine, they do not forgive sins, they do not give life, they do not create, they do not sanctify, they do not judge; rather, they are even judged. For “you,” he says, “will judge even angels” (1 Corinthians 6:3).

Nor are the powers of the heavens like this in themselves. They are not uncircumscribed by place, nor immeasurable in extent. For when Gabriel spoke with Daniel (Daniel 9:21-22), or brought the good news to the Mother of God …

choices.issue: Garbled draft with edition numbers and a split chapter title
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English printed 3.30, 3.31, 3.32 and '4.' in the text, used 'wherefore', and broke the chapter title of 4.ν across two paragraphs ('the angels, therefore, they say, are not...' / 'Are they from God'). It garbled 3.29 ('one God does not have a unified nature'; 'as it is the custom to speak to heretics'), 3.32 ('to take care not … to draw down the divine which is upon them'), 4.1 ('while they are being sent out, they are simple, direct, and perfect'), 4.2 ('impossible to be by Him through creation'), 4.4 ('subtilize themselves') and 4.6. Isaiah 7:9, which Didymus gives to Paul, is the Greek wording and is now marked LXX; '(1 Cor 3:19)' and '(1 Cor 6:3)' written in full; John 4:24, 1 Timothy 6:16 and Daniel 9:21-22 added; '[all]' removed.

choices.why: The section opens mid-phrase ('like and equal to the Father’s and' ends the previous section); only this section's words are translated.

choices.term: ἐπειδὴ μὴ συνηνωμένον ἔχει τὸ «εἷς θεός»
choices.english: since he does not have “one God” joined to his name
choices.why: Didymus turns the Macedonian rule of 3.21 on the Son: 'good' is never joined with 'one God' in his case either. 'to his name' makes the referent plain.
Didymus' apology for having to voice the blasphemous conclusion; kept as his hedge.

choices.english: was begotten together with his goodness / proceeded together with it
choices.why: The compounds say that goodness came with the begetting and the procession; the object is supplied from ἀγαθότητα in the same sentence.

The heretics' puzzle: if God is spirit (John 4:24), the Holy Spirit would be 'spirit of spirit'.
